summary.text: Earth's atmosphere is the layered mix of gases, commonly called air, that gravity holds around the planet.
It shields the surface from most meteoroids and ultraviolet sunlight, and keeps the surface warm by holding in heat through the greenhouse effect.
Dry air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and the atmosphere grows thinner with height, with no definite boundary where space begins.

facts.label: Main gas
facts.value: Nitrogen, 78.08% of dry air by molecules

facts.label: Where the mass sits
facts.value: Three-quarters within about 11 km of the surface

items.prompt: Land plants need air for photosynthesis and land animals need it to breathe. Which layer of the atmosphere holds air suited to both?

options.label: The troposphere
The stratosphere
The mesosphere
The exosphere

items.explain: Air that land plants can use for photosynthesis and land animals can breathe is found in the troposphere, the lowest layer.

items.prompt: Imagine Earth suddenly lost its atmosphere. What would happen to the gap between daytime and nighttime temperatures?

options.label: It would shrink, as heat escapes evenly
It would stay the same as it is now
It would widen, with harsher extremes
It would vanish into one steady temperature

items.explain: The atmosphere reduces the temperature swing between day and night, so without it those extremes would grow.

items.prompt: Earth's early air was dominated by gases like nitrogen and methane. What filled it with oxygen?

options.label: Volcanoes releasing it from deep rock
Bacteria releasing it through photosynthesis
Comets and meteoroids delivering it
Sunlight splitting apart nitrogen gas

items.explain: Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water and released oxygen as a byproduct, eventually turning the atmosphere oxidizing.

items.prompt: A rocket climbs steadily from the ground. At what point does it cross a sharp boundary between air and space?

options.label: At about 11 km, where the air runs out
At the ozone layer, where air stops
At exactly 100 km, the natural edge
Never; the air just thins out gradually

items.explain: The atmosphere thins with altitude and has no definite boundary with space; the 100 km Kármán line is only a convention.

items.prompt: In the outermost layer of the atmosphere, gas atoms are extremely spread out. What does that let them do?

options.label: Freeze together into small ice crystals
Bond tightly into new heavy molecules
Fly hundreds of km without hitting another
Glow brightly in ordinary visible light

items.explain: In the exosphere, atoms and molecules are so far apart that they can travel hundreds of kilometres without colliding.

items.prompt: Where in the lower atmosphere would you expect to find the most water vapor?

options.label: In the coldest parts of the air
In hot, humid air masses
Spread evenly at all temperatures
Only directly above the oceans

items.explain: Water vapor ranges from about 10 ppm in the coldest parts of the lower atmosphere to as much as 5% in hot, humid air masses.

pack.title: The Air Life Rebuilt
pack.question: How did Earth's air become the mix we breathe today?

beats.title: The Air Life Rebuilt
beats.hook: The oxygen in your lungs was not part of Earth's first air at all.

beats.prompt: Put these stages of Earth's atmosphere in order

items.label: Mostly hydrogen and helium from the solar nebula
Mostly nitrogen and methane, by the Archean eon
Oxygen builds up in the Great Oxygenation Event

beats.explain: The primordial atmosphere lost its hydrogen and helium, became nitrogen and methane by the Archean, was oxygenated at the end of the Archean, and further rounds of oxygenation gave today's air.

beats.prompt: Early bacteria start using sunlight to split water and fix carbon. Over a very long time, what builds up in the air?
beats.explain: Cyanobacteria released reactive dioxygen as a byproduct, and this steady release eventually turned the reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one.

choices.label: Methane, given off as waste
choices.feedback: These bacteria released dioxygen, which pushed the air toward an oxidizing state rather than adding methane.

choices.label: Hydrogen, freed from the split water
choices.feedback: The gas these bacteria released was oxygen, not hydrogen.

choices.label: Helium, made as the water breaks
choices.feedback: Helium was part of the first atmosphere and escaped; splitting water does not make it.

beats.prompt: Sort each gas into its group
beats.explain: Among the trace gases, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases, while neon, krypton and xenon are noble gases like argon.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Gravity holds a layer of gases around Earth.
That air gets thinner the higher you go.
So there is a sharp line where air stops and space begins.
For convenience, many treat 100 km as the edge of space.

beats.explain: The atmosphere has no definite boundary with outer space; the Kármán line at 100 km is only a conventional definition.

beats.idea: Earth's air changed from hydrogen and helium to nitrogen and methane, and then life's photosynthesis filled it with oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: A blanket of gas
paragraphs.text: Earth's atmosphere is a layered mix of gases, commonly called air, held around the planet by gravity. Like the atmospheres of other planets, it also carries varying amounts of suspended aerosols and particles that make clouds and haze. It gets thinner with height and has no sharp boundary with space, though the Kármán line at 100 km is often used as a conventional edge. Its total mass is about 5.15×10¹⁸ kg, and three-quarters of that sits within about 11 km of the ground.

paragraphs.heading: What it does for us
paragraphs.text: The atmosphere shields the surface from most meteoroids and from most ultraviolet radiation from the Sun. It narrows the gap between daytime and nighttime temperatures, and it keeps the surface warm by holding in heat through the greenhouse effect. Air currents carry heat and moisture from one region to another. It also supplies the chemical and climate conditions in which life can exist and evolve. Air fit for land plants to photosynthesize and land animals to breathe is found in the troposphere.

paragraphs.heading: What air is made of
paragraphs.text: Counted by molecules, dry air is 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus small amounts of trace gases. Water vapor varies, averaging around 1% at sea level and 0.4% across the whole atmosphere. In the lower atmosphere its share ranges from tiny amounts in the coldest regions up to 5% in hot, humid air masses, and other gases are usually quoted as shares of dry air, without water vapor. The trace gases include other greenhouse gases, chiefly carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone.

paragraphs.heading: An atmosphere that changed
paragraphs.text: Earth's first atmosphere was mostly hydrogen and helium gathered from the solar nebula. Over time it changed through gases escaping to space, volcanism, impacts and weathering. By the Archean eon it had become a second atmosphere dominated by nitrogen and methane. Then cyanobacteria, life forms that use sunlight to split water and give off oxygen, released oxygen so steadily that the atmosphere's chemistry changed for good, in an event called the Great Oxygenation Event. Later rounds of oxygenation produced today's air, dominated by nitrogen and oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: Layers and mixing
paragraphs.text: Scientists divide the atmosphere into layers by traits such as temperature and composition: the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere. Up to about 100 km, turbulence stirs the gases so their proportions stay the same. Between roughly 80 and 120 km, that stirring gradually gives way to molecular diffusion. This forms a region called the heterosphere, where lighter gases make up a growing share the higher you go.

paragraphs.heading: The ragged outer edge
paragraphs.text: The exosphere is the outermost layer, so thin that some scientists count it as part of interplanetary space instead. It starts at the exobase, the top of the thermosphere, which sits at about 500 km and rises to about 1,000 km when incoming solar radiation is stronger. Its outer limit is fuzzy: some authorities place it near 10,000 km, others near 190,000 km, about halfway to the Moon. The layer is mostly hydrogen at extremely low density, and its particles sit so widely spaced that each can cover hundreds of kilometres before bumping into another.
